title: In her words
summary: In short: Henry's granddaughter, Angela Wright, grew up with her grandad in her life until she was nearly fourteen. Here she remembers him in her own voice: what he wore, his rules, his lorry and his birds, bath night and Sunday lunch at 67 Southville, holidays in Weymouth, and the war that came back to him at the end.
contentNote: The last scene includes Angela's memories of her grandmother's death and of the war memories that troubled Henry in his last years.

scenes.title: Angela's grandad
scenes.intro: Angela Wright is Henry's granddaughter, the daughter of his only daughter, Joyce. These are her memories of him, recorded in her own voice in October 2026. Every recording has a full transcript, and nothing plays until you press play. Where a memory appears elsewhere in the exhibition, a link takes you there.

stories.title: What he wore
stories.body: Angela's first picture of her grandad: the flat cap, the boots and the belt, even on the beach.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: Some of my earliest memories of Grandad, Henry John Bowles, my mum's dad, was a kind man who always wore a flat cap out of doors and boot-type shoes, with his trousers held up with a belt. In the summer his shirt sleeves were always rolled up. I can't ever remember seeing him wear anything like jeans or a T-shirt.

Even when we went on holidays, he would sit on the beach with his shoes, socks, long trousers, shirt and cap on. I can't even remember him in trunks or going for a swim. Only occasionally did he take his shoes and socks off, roll up his trousers and have a paddle.

But then my grandma was the same: always a dress, stockings and shoes, which very occasionally would come off for her to have a paddle. They would both sit in deckchairs while we played on the sand and in the water. I don't even think they owned a swimming costume.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

stories.title: The eldest of twelve
stories.body: Henry's parents, Arthur and Eliza Ann Bowles, and their twelve children at Stoford.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: But I need to go back a bit. Grandad was the eldest of twelve children to Arthur and Eliza Bowles, my great-Granfy and Gran Bowles. There is a family photo of them with their twelve adult children outside their house at Yeovil Junction, Stoford. It was a small terraced house with possibly only three bedrooms. I can't imagine how crowded that must have been.
There was a newspaper report of him still digging ditches at the age of ninety. Both he and great-Gran were in their nineties when they died.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

see.label: The eldest of twelve, in chapter 1

stories.title: Three children
stories.body: Henry and Nell married in December 1918 and had three children: Gilbert, Joyce and Bill.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: Grandad and Grandma got married in December 1918. They had three children: Uncle Gilbert, who then married Auntie Phyllis; Joyce, who was always called "Joycie One-Name" by her youngest brother, and she hated it, because she only had that one name. She married my dad, Cyril Edward Bush. And Uncle William, known as Bill.
Uncle Gilbert died on 21 January 1948, and never saw his son John. Uncle Bill never married, and died on 28 January 1968. So that's just a bit of background history.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

scenes.title: Grandad's ways
scenes.intro: A strict man, a careful drinker, a driver who never took a test, and a man with his own way of telling other drivers what he thought.

stories.title: No bad language
stories.body: Henry would not have rudeness or swearing, especially in front of women and children, even from his own grown-up brothers and sisters.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: So back to my memories of my grandad. But in some ways it's also memories of my grandma too, as looking back they seem to come as a package. They were both so much part of my life as a young child, and until I was almost a teenager.

Grandad was a strong disciplinarian. He did not like rudeness, nor did he like bad language. In fact he would reprimand his adult siblings for bad behaviour, especially bad language if it was in front of women and children. And because of that, there were some brothers, and sisters too, that we only visited occasionally.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

see.label: Keeping them in line, in chapter 1

stories.title: The Bowles day out
stories.body: Two coaches full of Bowleses, and crates of beer in the boot.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: There were a couple of times that a big Bowles day outing took place. Two coaches had to be hired. On one of those trips I remember we went to Badbury Rings, near Wimborne. By then Gran and Granfy had died, but there were still twelve siblings and their wives or husbands, all their children, and their children too. I really can't remember how many of us there were, but the two coaches were full, including crates of beer and food in the boot.

Poor Grandad didn't seem to relax very much, and afterwards Mum said it was because he was worried about how his brothers would behave, having so much to drink. Grandad didn't drink a lot. But don't get me wrong, he enjoyed a beer or a cider, but he would never get drunk.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

see.label: The Bowles day out, in chapter 7

stories.title: The charabanc and the lorry
stories.body: One of Yeovil's first charabanc drivers, who never took a driving test, and a bet with his daughter over a lorry and trailer.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: I'm told that Grandad was one of the first men in Yeovil to drive a charabanc. I was also told that he never took a driving test, but he did teach a number of friends how to drive, and rumour has it they all passed first time. Although I don't recall seeing him actually drive a car.
At some point in his life he became a long-distance lorry driver, but I think it was more local journeys he was doing when he retired. I'm not sure.

On one occasion when my mum, Joycie One-Name, was on leave from the ATS during the Second World War, Grandad challenged her that if she could reverse park his lorry and trailer, he would give her half a crown. A lot of money back then, but only about 25p now. And he had to pay her up, because she did it perfectly.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

see.label: The charabanc and the lorries, in chapter 7

stories.title: "Hello then"
stories.body: How Henry let another driver know they had done something wrong.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: I remember it was Uncle Bill who was the first one in the family to own a car. Other than that, we would hire one for a week's holiday.

I can remember asking why Grandad would wind down the window and say "hello then" to another driver. When I asked if he knew them, he would say, "No, but they know what I mean." Then it was explained that the other driver had done something wrong, and by saying that, they then knew he was questioning what they had done. Can you imagine doing that today?
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026
stories.quote: No, but they know what I mean.

scenes.title: 67 Southville
scenes.intro: While Angela's father was away with the Navy during the Korean War and her mother went back to work, Angela spent her days with her grandparents at 67 Southville, Yeovil. "Those were just lovely days."

stories.title: The bird hospital
stories.body: Canaries and budgies in the old shed, two cages kept for the sick ones, and certificates from the Yeovil shows.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: Grandad also loved keeping canaries and budgies in his aviary, which was an old shed he had converted in his garden. He had two cages that he kept for any of the birds that became ill: his bird hospital, I was told.

I loved going in there to help him look after them, and felt really happy to be able to put seed and water into each cage. It was all measured out so that they didn't have too much. Grandad would then choose a few birds to put into a bird show in Yeovil. I can't remember how he got them to the show, because he didn't have a car, only a moped. He usually came away having won a few certificates for his birds. It was really special to do that with him.
He also belonged to the R.A.O.B., and was head of the lodge opposite the Salvation Army in Southville, Yeovil.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026
stories.quote: It was really special to do that with him.

stories.title: The kitchen motorbike
stories.body: Helping Grandma with the vegetables, riding pillion on a kitchen chair, and the belt that was never used.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: As I said earlier, Grandma and Grandad in my mind always came as a package, because I spent so much time at their house in my early years, when the Navy called Dad up for the Korean War. Mum had to go back to work part time as a home help, and I would go up to 67 Southville to be looked after until Mum got home. Those were just lovely days.

Most of my time was spent with Grandma, and I loved arriving in time to help her. In their kitchen they had a backless chair that my grandma used as a stool to sit on by the sink to do all the veg. She would sit forward, and I would sit behind her with my arms around her waist. Then this became a motorbike. And however she put up with me turning sharp corners, and then racing down the road to suddenly stop at the crossroads, I will never know. Things you do for your granddaughter.

If I was naughty I would be told to sit in the armchair with no books or toys, and to consider why I was sat there. Grandad would tell me that he would take his belt to me. That never happened. Just a movement of hand towards his belt was all that was needed to make me behave. Grandad never showed anything but love.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026
stories.quote: Grandad never showed anything but love.

see.label: The hand and the belt, in chapter 7

stories.title: Bath night
stories.body: Two rooms down, three bedrooms up, the toilet outside, and a tin bath in front of the fire.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: Grandma and Grandad lived in a terraced house at the top of Southville. It was two rooms downstairs and three bedrooms upstairs: two at the back, and one in the front, which was Grandma and Grandad's.

In the early days, even when I was a young child, there was no bathroom. The toilet was a room outside, and a tin bath hung on the wall, which was brought in in front of the fire when it was bath night. It was filled with hot water which had to be heated up in the copper, where the clothes were washed on a Monday. The whole family would then use the same bath water. You really didn't want to be the last person in the water, as it was almost cold, and by then you had everybody else's dirty water.

A bit later Grandma and Grandad had a bath put in the kitchen. Grandad made a hinged wooden cover to come down over it, to give another working surface. It was like that until we moved up the road from 25 to 67 after Grandad died, and my dad made the coal hole room and store cupboard into a bathroom. That was luxury. But the toilet was still outside.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

stories.title: Sunday lunch
stories.body: The front room, the table by the window, and how to lay it properly.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: The front room was also the dining room. It was set up so the table was at the back by the window, and the settee and chairs were up near the open fire. That was the extent of the downstairs living area.

Sunday lunches with Grandma and Grandad were a wonderful time. Uncle Bill was always there too, as he lived with them. Grandma was a good cook. She always let me lay the table, which had to be done properly. Grandma had been in service before she was married, and she made sure I was taught how a table should be laid every day, not just on special occasions. I still try to do that today.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

stories.title: With Grandma at the Army
stories.body: Nell took Angela to the Salvation Army, and to Thorpe's for fish and chips on a Saturday.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: I used to go to the Salvation Army with Grandma and sit with her in the morning meeting, and even in Weymouth on holiday we would go to the Corps there together, just her and me. It was Grandma that taught me about Jesus and how to trust Him. Even on school holidays I would go with her to her midweek ladies' services. All such precious times.
Grandma would sometimes take me to Thorpe's fish and chip shop for Saturday lunch, and of course we had to have bread and butter with it too. Even then we had to say grace before we could eat.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

scenes.title: Remembering
scenes.intro: The end of Nell's life, holidays by the sea for Henry's chest, the war that came back to him at the end, and Angela's thanks.

stories.title: Report day
stories.body: Opening the school report early at Grandma and Grandad's, and the only time Angela saw her grandad cry.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: Grandma and Grandad lived at 67 Southville, and we lived down the hill at 25. So on school report day it was handy having them living halfway between school and home. I would pop in to see them, as I did most days, and encourage them to open my report, so I would know what the marks were before I got home. Very helpful at times.

One day, after Grandma had been taken into hospital because she had cancer, I called in as usual to see Grandad. He was in the garden on his own. As I walked down the path I could see he was crying. That was the only time I saw him cry. Grandma had died that morning. A special time Grandad and I had together, hugging, just for a moment.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

stories.title: Weymouth
stories.body: The sea air and the flat Promenade were good for a man who had been gassed.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: Grandad had been gassed during the First World War in France, and since then had always had problems breathing. During the winter he would get bronchitis and chest infections. The air in Weymouth and the flatness of the Promenade were good for Grandad's health, so for a long time we would go there for our holidays.

Grandma and Grandad's next-door neighbours, Aunt Flo and Uncle Joe, would come too. We rented a flat above the shop on the Nothe side of the harbour. It was a wonderful time all together, and if the fishermen had any spare fish they would let us have them. On days when Grandad couldn't walk too far, he would have a chair on the harbour, and sit there and enjoy chatting to those passing by.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

stories.title: The barbed wire
stories.body: In his last years the war came back to Henry. Many years later, Angela walked the field where he was shot.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: Towards the end of Grandad's life he started being less tolerant. I started to have piano lessons, and because the piano was at 67, I would go up there to practise. Well, my lessons only lasted two weeks. Grandad couldn't stand the noise.

He also started having hallucinations, asking me to get the barbed wire off him, and stop people running all over him. Not until many years later, when I read the book Birdsong, did I understand what he must have gone through during the war.
[In August 2026 Angela and other members of Henry's family walked in his footsteps on the Somme.]

We spread out across the field and walked until our guide told us to stop. Our guide, Frank, told us that Grandad had walked, with the Somerset Light Infantry, on the first day of the Battle of the Somme, across that field. It was also the field where he was shot, thankfully only wounded, but where so many officers and comrades were killed or wounded.
Grandad died two days before my fourteenth birthday, on the 18th of January 1963.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026

stories.title: Thank you
stories.body: Angela's thanks, to her grandad and to all the young men like him.
stories.speaker: Angela
transcript: I, we, have so much to thank Grandad for, and all the young men like him. So many gave their lives. So many were badly wounded. So many were gassed and had health problems for the rest of their lives. So many kept all these experiences to themselves. They did this all for the freedom we have today. This is something we must never forget.

My grandma and grandad were the best grandparents a child could have. They always had time for me, and then later for my sister Sandra too. Nothing was ever too much trouble for us, for their family or friends. I loved my grandma and grandad so much. They taught me a lot, and hopefully, now I am a grandma to four beautiful girls, I can try and emulate them too.
Grandma and Grandad, thank you.
stories.source: Angela Wright, recorded for the exhibition, October 2026
stories.quote: This is something we must never forget.
